source: Wei et al. (2022) Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Few-shot prompts that show worked reasoning steps (eight exemplars) lift big models a lot. This is the machine version of a worked example.
numbers: PaLM 540B GSM8K 17.9% standard vs 56.9% with chain of thought (+39.0). Other sets: 69.4 to 79.0, 72.1 to 73.9, 25.2 to 35.8, 79.2 to 93.3. Same exemplars were written by authors; three other sets of eight exemplars sampled from the GSM8K train set also beat standard prompting.
limits: Gain appears only at large scale. Exemplar sets show some variance. Later work (c04, c05) shows the gain from exemplars has shrunk for newer models.
agent_relevance: Baseline: a worked example in context is the oldest scaffold. The open question is what part of it works (format, steps, or strategy).

source: Chen et al. (2023) How Many Demonstrations Do You Need for In-context Learning?
finding: Going from 7-8 demos to one random demo costs little. One demo that is known to be correct beats using all demos. This echoes the human finding that three examples did no better than one.
numbers: code-davinci-002, tasks from Wei et al. Cutting 7-8 demos to 1 random demo: accuracy drop only 0-7%. GSM8K: 83% of test items have at least one demo that gives the right answer; one positive demo gets about 83% vs about 60% with all 8 demos. Estimated accuracy of one random demo 52% GSM8K, 71% CSQA, matching the observed numbers.
limits: One model (code-davinci-002), old benchmarks the authors say are biased toward easy items. Finding a positive demo per query is the hard part; the model cannot do it alone.
agent_relevance: Supports retrieving ONE good matching worked example per task, not a pile. Selection quality matters more than count.

source: Chen et al. (2023) How Many Demonstrations Do You Need (positive vs negative demos)
finding: Adding more demos can hurt. Accuracy drops as positive demos are added to one positive demo on some items, and rises as negative demos are added. Authors read this as interference between demos.
numbers: Easy items (many positive demos) vs hard items: one positive demo reaches near 99% on easy GSM8K items; on hard items most demos lead to wrong answers (about 12.5% accuracy when at most 1 of 8 demos is positive).
limits: Mechanism is the authors' reading, not tested with attention or training probes.
agent_relevance: A wrong or mismatched example in the library can cost accuracy. Worked examples need a validity check before they enter memory.

source: Wang et al. (2025) From Harm to Help: Turning Reasoning In-Context Demos into Assets for Reasoning LMs
finding: For reasoning models, adding worked solutions from a strong teacher (DeepSeek-R1 traces, retrieved by similarity) lowers accuracy, and more examples lower it more. Two causes: the model copies steps from the example, and it fails to transfer the strategy.
numbers: AIME'25 one demo: drop of about 6-16 points; three demos: drop up to 35 points. GPQA-Diamond: 1-5 points at 1 shot, 4-8 points at 3 shots. Larger 32B distilled model also declines.
limits: Reasoning models trained with verifier RL; retrieved demos from OpenThoughts-114k. May not hold for non-reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Direct analogue of the human 'expertise reversal' and copy-the-example failure. Show the worked example only as an abstracted insight, not as a text to imitate.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Insight-to-Solve (I2S), same paper
finding: Fix for the copy problem: first turn the demos into explicit reusable insights, then write a target-specific solution, optionally self-refine. This is close to self-explanation of a worked example by the learner.
numbers: R1-Distill-Qwen-14B AIME25 direct 50.00 to I2S 54.00 to I2S+ 60.00; GPQA 59.50 to 59.60 (I2S) to 63.03 (I2S+). Qwen3-1.7B AIME25 35.96 to 41.32 (I2S) to 42.65 (I2S+). R1-Distill-Qwen-7B AIME25 42.00 to 48.00 to 51.33. Abstract: GPT-4.1 +14.0% on AIME'25. General reasoning gains smaller (e.g. 14B 'General' 57.68 to 66.64/68.40).
limits: Three small open models in the tables I read; I2S sometimes matches I2S+; gains on some splits are within a few points.
agent_relevance: Strongest evidence that a self-explanation step between the example and the new problem repairs the worked-example effect for LLMs. Use it as the retrieval-to-use step in the subgoal library.

source: Cheng et al. (2025) Revisiting Chain-of-Thought Prompting: Zero-shot Can Be Stronger than Few-shot
finding: For strong recent models (Qwen2.5), CoT exemplars no longer improve math reasoning over zero-shot CoT. Their main job is to fix the output format. Even exemplars written by stronger models (Qwen2.5-Max, R1) do not help. Attention analysis shows the model mostly ignores the exemplar content.
numbers: Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct GSM8K: 8-shot 95.75 vs zero-shot 91.58 vs zero-shot with fixed answer extraction 95.83. Qwen2.5-72B-Base GSM8K 90.52 vs 84.69 vs 90.27. MATH 81.30 vs 81.64 (instruct).
limits: Math tasks, Qwen family and similar. 'Zero-shot-Fix' result shows most of the apparent few-shot gain was an answer-parsing artifact.
agent_relevance: Warns that part of the old worked-example benefit in LLMs is format alignment, not learning. Our test must fix the parser before crediting examples.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Towards Understanding Chain-of-Thought Prompting: An Empirical Study of What Matters
finding: Worked examples with invalid reasoning still keep most of the gain. What matters is that steps are relevant to the query and in the right order. Correct arithmetic or logic inside the example matters much less.
numbers: text-davinci-002, GSM8K answer accuracy: standard 15.4, CoT 48.5, invalid reasoning 39.5 (about 81% of CoT), no relevance of bridging objects 27.5, no relevance at all 11.0. Over 90% of CoT intrinsic score retained with invalid reasoning.
limits: Older models; GSM8K and Bamboogle plus factual QA. Newer models may read content more carefully.
agent_relevance: Suggests the shape of the example (relevant, ordered subgoals) is what transfers. Supports storing subgoal skeletons rather than polished full solutions.

source: Min et al. (2022) Rethinking the Role of Demonstrations: What Makes In-Context Learning Work?
finding: Random labels in demonstrations barely hurt classification and multi-choice tasks across 12 models. What matters is label space, input distribution and format.
numbers: Small drop from gold to random labels: 2.6% absolute on average for classification; 12 models incl. GPT-3.
limits: Classification and multiple choice, not multi-step reasoning. Models are older.
agent_relevance: Parallel to the human result that the format and structure of an example carry the effect. Not evidence on solution correctness for reasoning tasks.

source: Bertsch et al. (2025) In-Context Learning with Long-Context Models: An In-Depth Exploration
finding: For classification with many labels, more examples keep helping up to thousands. Retrieval of a few well-matched examples is strong at low counts but gains flatten with more. This contrasts with the reasoning-task finding that more examples do not help.
numbers: Going from 10 to 1000 demonstrations gains up to 50.8 points, average 36.8 points across 5 datasets (Llama2-80k). Performance still rises past 2000 demos. Long context lessens the need to choose examples carefully.
limits: Classification and summarisation, not multi-step reasoning. Shows that 'three examples no better than one' is task-specific.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: the one-example rule applies to reasoning with worked solutions, not to pattern-labelling tasks.

source: Alazraki et al. (2025) No Need for Explanations: LLMs can implicitly learn from mistakes in-context (EMNLP 2025)
finding: Pairing wrong and right answers with NO explanation of the error beats explained pairs and beats chain of thought. Explicit corrective rationales over-constrain the model. This is a case where less explanation in the example works better.
numbers: Implicit prompting beats CoT in 85% of model x dataset x task combinations and explicit-rationale prompting in 88%. Averages: editing task +4.4% over CoT and +2.2% over explicit; solving +1.6 and +1.9 points; labelling F1 +5.6% over CoT and +6.2% over explicit. Datasets: GSM8K, ASDiv, AQUA, PRM800K; many models; five-run averages.
limits: Math reasoning only. Human evaluation of rationales the models generate themselves was lower quality for implicit prompting.
agent_relevance: Incorrect-vs-correct contrast pairs (error-example research in humans) work for models too. Store failed attempts next to the fix without long explanations.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) In-Context Principle Learning from Mistakes (LEAP)
finding: Model is made to fail on the few-shot examples, reflects on the mistakes, and writes principles. The principles plus the same examples improve answers. This is self-explanation of worked examples plus error analysis, with no extra examples.
numbers: GPT-4: DROP few-shot CoT 72.05 to LEAP 79.55 (low-level) / 78.60 (high-level); HotpotQA 36.35 to 39.30 / 39.65. GPT-3.5: DROP 63.20 to 63.35 / 63.00. In 37 of 42 task x model combinations on BBH one LEAP variant beat few-shot CoT. Llama-2-chat-70B: GSM8K 52.5 to 50.6 / 47.0 (worse), MATH 16.2 to 13.8 / 14.2 (worse), even with GPT-4 principles.
limits: Weak models (Llama-2 70B, Gemini Pro on HotpotQA) do not use the principles and can lose accuracy. Gains are model-strength dependent.
agent_relevance: Self-explanation helps only when the model is strong enough to use it. Gate the step by model strength.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models
finding: Skill library of verified, executable code, retrieved by description embedding, is a library of worked solutions that compounds. A skill is stored only after self-verification confirms the task is done.
numbers: 3.3x more unique items, 2.3x longer distances, tech tree milestones up to 15.3x faster than prior SOTA. Tech tree (160-iteration cap, 3 runs): Diamond tool reached by Voyager 1/3 (102 iterations); Voyager without skill library 0/3; AutoGPT, ReAct, Reflexion 0/3. Iron tool 21 +- 7 iterations with library vs 29 +- 11 without.
limits: GPT-4 in Minecraft via a high-level API; small trial counts (3 per method). Early tiers (wooden, stone) show no benefit from the library.
agent_relevance: The closest working agent version of a subgoal library as worked examples. Gains show up only on the deep tiers where reuse compounds.

source: Yang et al. (2024) Buffer of Thoughts: Thought-Augmented Reasoning with Large Language Models
finding: Stores high-level thought templates distilled from solved problems and instantiates one for each new problem. It stores the abstraction of a worked example, not the example.
numbers: GPT-4 table: Game of 24 82.4 vs standard 3.0, CoT 11.0, ToT 74.0; Checkmate-in-One 86.4 vs 36.4 standard, ToT 49.2; Geometric Shapes 93.6 vs 52.6; Python Puzzles 52.4 vs 31.1; Date Understanding 88.2 vs 68.4. Cost about 12% of multi-query methods. Abstract: Llama3-8B plus BoT may surpass Llama3-70B.
limits: Self-reported by the method's authors on 10 tasks; templates for similar problem types, so gains concentrate on algorithmic tasks like Game of 24 and Checkmate.
agent_relevance: Matches the human finding that worked examples work best in algorithmic domains. Test our library on algorithmic ARC-type items first.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: Agent induces reusable workflows (sub-routines) from past successes and injects them for new tasks. Works offline from training examples or online from test queries.
numbers: Relative success rate +24.6% on Mind2Web (step-wise, cross-task) and +51.1% on WebArena over the best published autonomous method (GPT-4, temperature 0). AWM WebArena total success 35.5% (table row; step counts reported as fewer than baseline). Beats methods with human-written workflows by 7.9%. Online AWM beats baselines by 8.9 to 14.0 absolute points as train-test gap widens.
limits: Web navigation only; workflow induction quality is model dependent; benchmark leakage not studied in the parts I read.
agent_relevance: A subgoal library that grows online and generalises across tasks and domains; the gap widening with distance supports abstract rather than literal examples.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners
finding: Agent gathers success and failure trajectories, extracts natural-language insights by comparing failure with success, and recalls successful trajectories as in-context examples. Each channel helps in different domains.
numbers: Insights-only vs retrieval-only: HotpotQA 36% vs 31%; ALFWorld 50% vs 55%. ALFWorld with Reflexion rounds R0 to R3: ExpeL retrieve-only 40.3% to 54.4%; ExpeL plus insights 54.5% to 60.4% (best row 59.0% to 64.2%). Transfer to FEVER: ReAct 58%, ExpeL without task demos 63%, ExpeL transfer 65%, best 70%.
limits: Needs training tasks and success/failure pairs; diverse failure data from Reflexion beat ReAct-only data.
agent_relevance: Both retrieval of full worked trajectories and abstracted insights are useful. Knowledge-heavy tasks gain from insights, action-heavy ones from trajectories.

source: Lekshmi-Narayanan et al. (2024) Explaining Code Examples in Introductory Programming Courses: LLM vs Humans
finding: ChatGPT can write line-by-line explanations for worked code examples. Its explanations are closer to expert ones than student-written ones, but harder to read.
numbers: 4 programs, 33 code lines; 12 ChatGPT explanation sets (simple/advanced/extended prompts), 2 expert sets, 60 student explanations. Gunning Fog medians: students 8.02, experts 8.46, ChatGPT simple 8.67, advanced 9.91, extended 11.09; difference across sources p<0.001; extended vs experts p=0.0102. ChatGPT vs expert similarity higher than student vs expert (Mann-Whitney p<0.05 on METEOR, USE, BERTScore). Simple prompt aligned better with experts than the extended one.
limits: Tiny expert sample (N=2); no learning outcome measured; ChatGPT version not stated in the part I read.
agent_relevance: Authoring cost of worked examples can be cut by a model, but check for over-long explanations; the simple prompt matched experts best.

source: Gonzaga, Vassar, Jiang (2026) CS Teaching Assistant Perceptions on LLM-Generated Faded Worked Examples for Feedback Training (SIGCSE TS 2026)
finding: Randomised trial of an LLM tool that gives faded worked examples to teaching assistants. Faded examples gave no significant cognitive-load advantage over the standard tool.
numbers: N=27 TAs; mixed methods; no effect sizes or p-values on the page I opened.
limits: Very small N, page gives only the summary; TAs are not novices to the content; outcome is load and perception, not learning.
agent_relevance: A weak, failed replication of the fading advantage when the learner is not a novice. Consistent with expertise reversal.

source: Bastani et al. (2025) Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics (PNAS 122(26))
finding: Students given full-answer GPT-4 during practice scored far higher in practice but worse on a later test without it. A tutor tuned to withhold answers and give hints removed most of the harm. Echoes: giving the finished solution too freely is not the same as studying a worked example with self-explanation.
numbers: Nearly 1,000 high school students (exact N not in abstract). Practice grades +48% (GPT Base) and +127% (GPT Tutor). Later exam without access: GPT Base 17% worse than control; GPT Tutor about equal to control.
limits: Abstract page only was opened, not the full paper. Secondary coverage says the Tutor condition did not beat control, so it mitigated harm rather than adding learning.
agent_relevance: Tells us what happens when the 'learner' leans on a solver. For our agent: do not let a retrieved solution replace its own attempt; keep it as a hint.

source: Puech et al. (2025) Towards the Pedagogical Steering of LLMs for Tutoring: Modeling Productive Failure (Findings of ACL 2025)
finding: Default GPT-4o tutors give away the solution; a prompt-optimisation method (StratL) with a transition graph of tutor intents keeps the tutor in a problem-first strategy. The opposite pole to worked examples.
numbers: Field study 17 high school students in Singapore; two 9th grade math problems solved by 62% of students. StratL produced a significantly higher PF Score than the baseline (2-sample t-test) and elicited on average 2.6 solution methods per session vs fewer for the baseline (p=.05). No learning-gain test.
limits: N=17, one problem type, no posttest. Productive failure and worked-example effects compete; this study does not compare them for learning.
agent_relevance: Shows how to steer a model's behaviour with a code-held plan of intents; also the cue that there is a design choice: show solution first or last.

source: Cheng et al. (2025) Revisiting CoT, attention analysis
finding: Authors argue the 'strong model' test is whether zero-shot CoT beats few-shot CoT. Strong models skip exemplar content and follow instructions. Earlier few-shot gains came from weaker models with poor zero-shot ability.
numbers: Version 3 dated 8 Jan 2026. Fixed-parser zero-shot (GSM8K Qwen2.5-72B-Base) 90.27 vs 8-shot 90.52, a 0.25 point gap.
limits: Math only; the claim is about models, not learners.
agent_relevance: Parallel to expertise reversal: examples help weak solvers and add little for strong ones. Condition example use on the model's own zero-shot success.

source: Bertsch et al. (2025) Long-context ICL: retrieval vs fixed examples
finding: Retrieving matched examples per test item is far better at small counts; the benefit shrinks as the number of demonstrations grows. Grouping same-label examples hurts.
numbers: Retrieval with BM25 gives 78-95% on the classification sets at small k in Table 2; the gap between retrieval and plain many-shot shrinks at large counts. Long-context fine-tuned Llama-2-7b up to 80K tokens.
limits: Classification-focused.
agent_relevance: For a small library, retrieve by match; order and grouping matter.

source: Alazraki et al. (2025) No Need for Explanations: why it works
finding: Incorrect answers help more than adding extra diverse correct answers. Explanations cost context length and the model overfits to their wording.
numbers: Authors compare context length, answer diversity and n-gram overlap between exemplars and outputs; explicit-rationale prompting copies more of the exemplar wording.
limits: Details of the overfit numbers (Table 3) not copied in full.
agent_relevance: Short contrast pairs may beat long explained solutions as library entries.

source: Wei et al. (2022) Chain-of-Thought, annotator robustness
finding: Different annotators' exemplar sets and sets sampled from training data all beat standard prompting, with some variance across sets. Authors ran concise versions of the chain too.
numbers: Three further sets of eight exemplars sampled from the GSM8K training set, and two further annotators (co-authors A and B) in addition to the original; all beat standard prompting.
limits: Same family of models; variance is reported across sets.
agent_relevance: The benefit does not depend on one author's examples, but picking among sets still matters.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Towards Understanding CoT: error types
finding: With invalid demonstrations, the model still writes valid reasoning for the new question. Its errors fall into the same types as under normal CoT. Order of steps matters: shuffled steps cost accuracy.
numbers: Authors examined 20 GSM8K items where CoT was right and invalid-reasoning wrong, and 20 for the reverse; error categories were similar between the two.
limits: Small manual error analysis (40 items).
agent_relevance: Model does its own reasoning; the example sets the frame. Do not expect the example's logic to be copied.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) LEAP: low-level vs high-level principles
finding: Task-specific principles come in two kinds, low-level (what went wrong in each example) and high-level (general guidance). Neither dominates. LEAP needs no more examples than ordinary few-shot.
numbers: GPT-4 DROP 79.55 low-level vs 78.60 high-level; Gemini Pro DROP 67.15 vs 67.60; GPT-4 HotpotQA 39.30 vs 39.65.
limits: Differences between the two kinds are within noise.
agent_relevance: Either level of self-explanation is enough; pick the cheaper.

source: Voyager ablation on curriculum and skill retrieval
finding: Baselines that accumulate no reusable skills (ReAct, Reflexion, AutoGPT-style) stall in deep tasks. Skill reuse matters most when tasks build on each other.
numbers: Wooden tool: Voyager 6 +- 2 iterations, without library 7 +- 2, AutoGPT 92 +- 72; Stone tool 11 +- 2 vs 9 +- 4 (library slightly slower); 3 trials each.
limits: Three trials per method, so differences in early tiers are noise.
agent_relevance: Expect zero or negative effect of a library on simple items and a gain only on compositional ones; measure by depth.
